props.title: Total Eclipse

sections.content: **Total Eclipse** (1995) stands as a raw, unflinching portrayal of the turbulent relationship between French poets Arthur Rimbaud and Paul Verlaine, with Leonardo DiCaprio delivering a breakthrough performance as the teenage Rimbaud. The film follows similar territory as **Bright Star** (2009) and **Carrington** (1995) in its exploration of artistic passion and destructive love, but director Agnieszka Holland pushes further into the darkness of creative obsession. Like **Amadeus** (1984), it shows genius as both gift and curse, though with a grittier, more sexually charged energy.

sections.content: The mid-1990s saw a surge of period dramas focused on tortured artists and writers, including **Restoration** (1995) and **Love and Death on Long Island** (1997). What sets **Total Eclipse** apart is its refusal to romanticize its subjects. Holland presents Rimbaud's genius and cruelty with equal weight, much like Peter Greenaway's approach in **The Draughtsman's Contract** (1982). The film's frank depiction of same-sex desire was groundbreaking for its time, predating mainstream works like **Gods and Monsters** (1998).

DiCaprio's performance as Rimbaud showcases the same intensity he would later bring to **The Basketball Diaries** (1995) and **Romeo + Juliet** (1996). His portrayal of creative genius mixed with teenage arrogance creates an electric tension with David Thewlis's more restrained Verlaine. This dynamic recalls the volatile relationships in **Prick Up Your Ears** (1987) and **Vincent & Theo** (1990). SUBHEAD: The Poetry of Cinema

sections.content: Holland's direction employs a visual language that mirrors Rimbaud's revolutionary poetry. Like Derek Jarman's **Caravaggio** (1986), the film uses period authenticity as a foundation for exploring modern themes. The candlelit scenes and rain-slicked streets of 19th-century Paris create an atmosphere reminiscent of **The Piano** (1993), where passion and creativity exist in opposition to societal constraints.
